passage: The placement cell corridor smelled of floor cleaner and nerves. Parul sat on a plastic chair with her folder on her knees, watching the door of Room 4 where Harish, her classmate, had just gone in for his interview. Her own turn was after lunch. She felt a flutter of hope and a heavy dread at once, and her leg would not stop bouncing. The coordinator, passing with a stack of forms, noticed and said, "Write down the three questions you fear most and one line for each." Parul tore a page from her notebook and wrote. Seeing them on paper made them smaller. When Harish came out grinning and shaking his hand out, she stood, straightened her folder and walked toward the water cooler, her list in her pocket.

qa.q: Which door was Parul watching while she waited?
qa.a: She was watching the door of Room 4, where Harish had just gone in.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling while she waited, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt both hope and dread, shown by her bouncing leg, though the nerves might simply mean she cares about the outcome.

qa.q: What small step helped Parul?
qa.a: Writing down her three most feared questions with a line for each made them feel smaller and gave her something to do.

qa.q: How might Harish's grin look to Parul?
qa.a: It may add to her hope or to her worry, since one good interview does not tell her how hers will go.

grounding: Parul feels hope and dread before a placement interview and turns dread into a small plan.

subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]
passage:
Dear Jatin,

You asked how I'm feeling about moving to Bengaluru next month, so here is the honest answer: excited and scared, taking turns. The excited part imagines the new job and my own flat. The scared part keeps asking, what if I can't manage? Last night I got tired of both and made a list instead. Find a room near the office, ask Uncle Rao about the first week, save the number for the landlord, pack the winter jacket. Then I emailed my new manager to ask what the first day looks like. She wrote back kindly within the hour. I still feel the dread, but now it has steps.

Come visit when I've a sofa.

Amandeep

qa.q: Where is Amandeep moving?
qa.a: Amandeep is moving to Bengaluru.

qa.q: What do the two feelings Amandeep describes look like, and what shifted them?
qa.a: Amandeep alternates between excitement about the new job and flat and fear of not managing, and making a list and emailing the new manager gave the dread steps.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do if the dread stayed strong?
qa.a: Amandeep could keep breaking it into small steps and talk to someone trusted, such as Uncle Rao or a mentor.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Jatin may feel touched that Amandeep answered honestly, and possibly glad to be asked to visit.

grounding: Amandeep writes of hope and dread about a move and turns them into concrete steps and a mentor's help.

subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]
passage: Vishal, you asked me to talk about placement season for your college radio show, so here's the honest version. I'm Rekha. Two months before placements, I'd wake up at 4 a.m. with my heart racing. Half of me was hopeful: I'd worked hard, my projects were good. The other half was pure dread: what if nobody picks me, what if I freeze, what will Papa say? The dread was vague and huge. So I did something my senior Meenal suggested. I wrote the dread down as a list. "Freeze in interviews" became "do three mock interviews". "No company picks me" became "apply to twelve, not four". "Papa" became "talk to Papa this Sunday". I went to my faculty mentor with the list, and she helped me pick which companies suited me. Each small step made the dread smaller. I still felt nervous on the day. But it was nervous with a plan.

qa.q: How many companies did Rekha decide to apply to?
qa.a: Twelve, not four.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling in the two months before placements?
qa.a: Rekha felt both hopeful about the hard work and full of dread about freezing or not being picked, waking at 4 a.m. with a racing heart.

qa.q: What helped Rekha turn dread into action?
qa.a: Writing the fears as a list, turning each into a small step, and going to the faculty mentor for help choosing companies.

qa.q: How did Meenal's suggestion help?
qa.a: Meenal's idea of writing the dread down as a list gave Rekha a way to break vague fear into manageable steps.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing placements with hope and dread and using planning, mentors and small steps to make it manageable.

subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]
passage: I'm Aditi, and I shared a flat with Mridul in the months before he moved to Berlin for his master's. Some days he was glowing: he'd show me photos of the university, plan cycling routes, practise German on the balcony. Other days he'd sit on the sofa staring at the visa papers, not moving for an hour. Once I heard him say to himself, "What if I can't do it?" I didn't know exactly what was going on inside him. But I noticed that the stuck days got fewer after he made a big chart on the wall: visa, flat, bank account, course reading, one line for each week. He called a senior who had studied there, and they talked for an hour. After that he ticked something off the chart almost every day. The night before he left, he said, "I'm still scared. But now I know what Monday looks like."

qa.q: Where was Mridul moving for his master's?
qa.a: To Berlin.

qa.q: What might Mridul have been feeling on the days he stared at the visa papers?
qa.a: He seemed apprehensive and overwhelmed, wondering if he could do it, even though on other days he was hopeful and excited.

qa.q: What helped Mridul turn dread into action?
qa.a: A wall chart breaking the move into weekly tasks, and a long talk with a senior who had studied there.

qa.q: How does Aditi see the change in Mridul?
qa.a: Aditi noticed the stuck days getting fewer once he had the chart and started ticking things off, though Aditi couldn't know exactly what he felt.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult facing a move with hope and dread, and planning and mentors making it manageable.

passage:
Week one. Farida's final exams were a month away. She lay awake picturing failing everything, then picturing topping the class. Hope and dread in the same hour. She couldn't start studying; the pile of books just sat there.
Week two. She went to her tutor, Gautam sir, and admitted she was stuck. He didn't lecture. He asked her to split each subject into topics and write them on index cards, then pick three cards a day. "Just three. Not the whole mountain." She tried it. The first day she finished two. The second, three.
Week four. The night before the first exam, she still felt butterflies. But the index card box was almost empty, and she'd made notes for each topic. She texted Gautam sir: "Still nervous. But it feels like the good kind now." He replied, "Good. Nervous means you care. Sleep."

qa.q: How many cards did Gautam sir ask Farida to pick each day?
qa.a: Three cards a day.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling in week one?
qa.a: She felt both hopeful and full of dread, lying awake and unable to start studying.

qa.q: What small steps helped Farida move from dread to action?
qa.a: Talking to her tutor, splitting subjects into topics on index cards, and doing three a day.

qa.q: How did Gautam sir see Farida's nervousness at the end?
qa.a: He saw it as a sign she cared, and told her to sleep.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing exams with hope and dread, and a mentor and small steps turning dread into manageable action.

subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]
passage: Devika beta, you keep saying you can't sleep because of placement season, so let your Raghav chacha tell you about 1994. I was twenty-one, in my final year at the polytechnic in Nashik, and every night I'd lie awake, half dreaming of a job in Bombay, half sure I'd fail every interview and disappoint my father. Hope in one hand, dread in the other, and both too heavy. One evening my lecturer, Mr Sathe, found me staring at the notice board. He didn't give a speech. He said, "Write down five companies. Next to each, one thing you can do this week." So I did: one letter, one mock interview with him, one visit to a senior who worked at a factory in Satpur. Small things. The dread didn't vanish, but now it had something to hold. I didn't get my first choice. I got the third, and that's where I met your chachi, so no complaints.

qa.q: Where did Raghav Chacha study?
qa.a: At the polytechnic in Nashik.

qa.q: What was young Raghav feeling during those sleepless nights?
qa.a: He felt hopeful about a job in Bombay and, at the same time, full of dread about failing and disappointing his father.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Raghav manage the dread?
qa.a: Following Mr Sathe's suggestion to list five companies with one small step each that week, such as a letter, a mock interview and a visit to a senior.

qa.q: How might Mr Sathe have seen young Raghav at the notice board?
qa.a: As a worried student who needed practical steps more than a speech, which is why he offered a simple plan.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult facing placements with both hope and dread, and turning vague dread into manageable action through small steps and a mentor.
